title: Peripheral refraction with Eyhance versus Eyhance Pro intraocular lenses
official: Prospective, randomised, contralateral comparative study of peripheral refraction after implantation of an enhanced monofocal and an enhanced monofocal with improved peripheral vision intraocular lenses
summary:
Background and study aims
When cataract surgery is performed, the cloudy natural lens is replaced with an artificial lens called an intraocular lens (IOL). The TECNIS Eyhance IOL is an enhanced monofocal lens that provides excellent distance vision and improved intermediate vision (such as for computer use and cooking) compared to standard lenses. Johnson & Johnson has recently introduced a newer version called the TECNIS Eyhance Pro IOL, which is designed to additionally improve peripheral (side) vision while maintaining the same central vision quality. Both lenses are approved for routine NHS use and have excellent safety profiles.
This study aims to compare how these two lenses perform, particularly regarding peripheral vision. The study will recruit patients who need cataract surgery in both eyes. Each patient will receive one type of lens in one eye and the other type in the other eye (randomly allocated). This contralateral design eliminates differences between patients and allows direct comparison.

At one month after surgery, their peripheral vision will be measured using a specialised instrument (Grand Seiko WAM-5500 autorefractor), along with distance and intermediate vision, and ask patients about their visual experiences using questionnaires. The research assessments are entirely non-invasive and painless. This study will provide the first objective evidence of whether the newer Eyhance Pro lens truly offers advantages in peripheral vision compared to the standard Eyhance lens. The findings will inform lens selection for future cataract patients and advance understanding of how lens design influences peripheral visual performance

Who can participate?
Adults over 18 years old who require cataract surgery in both eyes.

What does the study involve?
Both eyes will be operated on the same day by experienced cataract surgeons. The surgery will be performed using the standard phacoemulsification technique (which uses ultrasound waves to break up and remove the cataract) with local anaesthesia (topical or sub-Tenon’s). A small incision will be made, the cataract removed, and the IOL implanted in the lens capsule. The surgical technique and safety profile are identical to those of standard NHS cataract surgery. Participants will have a follow-up at 1 month after their surgery where they will conduct some research tests including visual acuity testing (testing with one eye closed and the other open, for each eye separately), refraction (determining if they need glasses), peripheral refraction measurements (primary research assessment), clinical examination and questionnaires.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating
Benefits: 
Participants will receive two high-quality enhanced monofocal IOLs (either Eyhance or Eyhance Pro in each eye), both of which provide excellent distance vision and improved intermediate vision compared to standard monofocal lenses
•	They will have thorough eye examinations at the 1-month research visit
•	They will have the opportunity to directly compare two advanced lens technologies
•	They may contribute to advancing knowledge that will benefit future cataract patients
The information obtained from this study will help:
•	Determine whether the Eyhance Pro IOL offers measurable advantages in peripheral vision to improve peripheral visibility, which can help activities like driving and help patients with reduced central vision due to conditions like macular degeneration.
•	Inform IOL selection and patient counselling for future cataract patients
•	Advance our understanding of how IOL optical design influences peripheral visual performance
•	Provide evidence for systematic reviews (comprehensive analyses of all available research evidence to guide medical practice) and clinical guidelines
Risks: 
The general risks associated with any cataract surgery apply to this study. including:
•	Infection (endophthalmitis): very rare, approximately 1 in 1,000-3,000 cases
•	Inflammation
•	Bleeding
•	Retinal complications (such as retinal detachment)
•	Cystoid macular oedema (swelling at the back of the eye)
•	Posterior capsule opacification (clouding of the lens capsule requiring laser treatment)
•	Corneal complications
•	Refractive surprise (final glasses prescription different from target)
There are no additional surgical risks related to participating in this study. Both the Eyhance and Eyhance Pro IOLs are approved for NHS use and have excellent safety profiles identical to standard monofocal lenses.
Research-Related Risks
The research assessments (peripheral refraction measurements, iTrace scans, questionnaires) are:
•	Non-invasive and painless
•	Carry no additional risks

Where is the study run from?
Sussex Eye Hospital, UK.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
The study is open to recruitment as of October 2026. Planned study end date is December 2027.

Who is funding the study?
Johnson & Johnson

Who is the main contact?
Professor Mayank Nanavaty, mayank.nanavaty@nhs.net
criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Adults aged 18 years and over
2. Bilateral cataracts scheduled for routine cataract surgery on both eyes
3. Potential for good postoperative visual acuity (no significant ocular comorbidity)
4. Able to provide written informed consent
5. Able to attend the research follow-up visit at 1 month postoperatively.
Exclusion criteria:
1. Amblyopia (lazy eye)
2. Eyes with any ocular comorbidity with cornea, uvea, retina or optic nerve, which may be detrimental to visual outcomes
3. Previous ocular refractive surgery
sponsor: University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust
